title: Venn Diagrams & Sets
description: Use Venn diagrams to show sets, intersections, unions and complements.

notes.heading: What is a Set?

illustration.alt: Venn diagram showing a universal set U containing two overlapping circles labelled A and B.
illustration.caption: A Venn diagram shows how sets overlap inside a universal set.

notes.body:
📌 Definition
A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects called elements. Sets are usually named with capital letters such as $A$, $B$ or $U$.

We can write a set by listing its elements inside braces:
$$A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$$

The symbol $\in$ means "is an element of". For this set, $2 \in A$ and $5 \notin A$.

🔑 Key Concept
The universal set $U$ contains every object being considered in a problem. All other sets are drawn inside $U$.

💡 Worked Example
If $U = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ and $A = \{2, 4, 6\}$, list the elements that are in $U$ but not in $A$.

Answer: $1$, $3$, $5$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A set collects distinct objects.
• Capital letters name sets.
• $U$ is the universal set.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing $A \in 2$ instead of $2 \in A$. The element belongs to the set, not the set to the element.

notes.heading: Reading a Venn Diagram
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A Venn diagram uses closed curves, usually circles or rectangles, to represent sets and their relationships.

In a basic two-set Venn diagram:
• The rectangle represents the universal set $U$.
• Each circle represents one set.
• Points inside a circle are elements of that set.
• The overlapping region belongs to both sets.

🔑 Key Concept
An element that belongs to two sets is placed inside the overlap of their circles.

💡 Worked Example
Let $U = \{1, 2, 3, \dots, 10\}$, $A = \{2, 4, 6, 8, 10\}$ and $B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$.

Place each number in the diagram:
• $2$ and $4$ are in $A \cap B$, so they go in the overlap.
• $6, 8, 10$ are in $A$ only.
• $1, 3, 5$ are in $B$ only.
• $7, 9$ are outside both circles.

✅ Check
Every element of $U$ appears exactly once in the diagram.

notes.heading: Intersection $A \cap B$
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The intersection of two sets $A$ and $B$, written $A \cap B$, is the set of elements that are in both $A$ and $B$.

In symbols:
$$A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$$

🔑 Key Concept
In a Venn diagram, $A \cap B$ is the overlapping lens-shaped region of the two circles.

💡 Worked Example
If $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and $B = \{3, 4, 5, 6\}$, then:
$$A \cap B = \{3, 4\}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $A \cap B$ contains only the elements shared by both sets.
• If two sets have no elements in common, $A \cap B = \emptyset$.
• The order does not matter: $A \cap B = B \cap A$.

notes.heading: Union $A \cup B$
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The union of two sets $A$ and $B$, written $A \cup B$, is the set of all elements that are in $A$, in $B$, or in both.

In symbols:
$$A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$$

🔑 Key Concept
In a Venn diagram, $A \cup B$ covers everything inside either circle, including the overlap.

💡 Worked Example
If $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ and $B = \{3, 4, 5, 6\}$, then:
$$A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$$

✅ Check
Each element is listed only once, even if it appears in both sets.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Listing shared elements twice. Sets contain distinct objects, so $3$ and $4$ appear only once in $A \cup B$.

notes.heading: Complement $A'$
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The complement of a set $A$, written $A'$, is the set of all elements in the universal set $U$ that are not in $A$.

In symbols:
$$A' = \{x : x \in U \text{ and } x \notin A\}$$

🔑 Key Concept
In a Venn diagram, $A'$ is everything inside the rectangle $U$ but outside circle $A$.

💡 Worked Example
Let $U = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$ and $A = \{2, 4, 6, 8\}$.

Then:
$$A' = \{1, 3, 5, 7\}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The complement depends on the universal set $U$.
• $A \cap A' = \emptyset$.
• $A \cup A' = U$.

notes.heading: Subsets and Disjoint Sets
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A set $A$ is a subset of $B$, written $A \subset B$, if every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$.

Two sets are disjoint if they have no elements in common, so $A \cap B = \emptyset$.

🔑 Key Concept
In a Venn diagram:
• If $A \subset B$, the circle for $A$ sits completely inside the circle for $B$.
• If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, the two circles do not overlap.

💡 Worked Example
Let $A = \{2, 4\}$ and $B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$. Since every element of $A$ is in $B$, we write $A \subset B$.

Let $C = \{7, 8\}$. Then $A$ and $C$ are disjoint because $A \cap C = \emptyset$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Thinking that $A \subset B$ means $A$ and $B$ merely share some elements. It means every element of $A$ is in $B$.

notes.heading: Counting with Venn Diagrams
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The number of elements in a set $A$ is written $n(A)$.

For two sets, the counting rule is:
$$n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$$

🔑 Key Concept
We subtract $n(A \cap B)$ because those elements are counted twice when we simply add $n(A)$ and $n(B)$.

💡 Worked Example
In a group of students, $12$ play football, $9$ play basketball and $5$ play both. How many students play at least one sport?

Let $F$ be the set of football players and $B$ the set of basketball players.

$$n(F \cup B) = 12 + 9 - 5 = 16$$

So $16$ students play at least one sport.

✅ Check
Only the students in the overlap are subtracted once.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $n(A)$ means "the number of elements in set $A$".
• Add the two sets, then subtract the overlap.
• Use the diagram to fill in each region before adding.

notes.heading: Solving Problems with Venn Diagrams
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A Venn diagram can help organise information and answer questions about overlapping groups.

🔑 How it works
1. Draw a rectangle for the universal set $U$ and circles for each set.
2. Fill in the overlap first, using the number given for $A \cap B$.
3. Fill in the remaining parts of each circle.
4. Find the value asked for, such as total in $A \cup B$ or outside both sets.

💡 Worked Example
In a class of $30$ students, $18$ study Spanish, $15$ study French and $7$ study both. How many study neither language?

Step 1: Fill in the overlap: $7$.

Step 2: Spanish only: $18 - 7 = 11$.

Step 3: French only: $15 - 7 = 8$.

Step 4: Total inside at least one circle: $11 + 7 + 8 = 26$.

Step 5: Neither: $30 - 26 = 4$.

Answer: $4$ students study neither language.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to subtract the overlap before finding "only Spanish" or "only French".

flashcards.definition: A well-defined collection of distinct objects called elements.
flashcards.example: $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ is a set with three elements.

flashcards.definition: A single object that belongs to a set.
flashcards.example: For $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$, the number $2$ is an element of $A$, written $2 \in A$.

flashcards.definition: The set that contains all objects being considered in a problem.
flashcards.example: If only whole numbers from $1$ to $10$ are being considered, then $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 10\}$.

flashcards.definition: A diagram that uses overlapping shapes to show how sets are related.
flashcards.example: Two overlapping circles inside a rectangle show sets $A$ and $B$ inside the universal set $U$.

flashcards.definition: The set of elements that are in both sets.
The set of all elements that are in either set, or in both.
The set of all elements in the universal set that are not in a given set.
A set whose elements are all contained in another set.
flashcards.example: $\{2, 4\} \subset \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ because every element is in the larger set.

flashcards.definition: Two sets that have no elements in common.
flashcards.example: $\{1, 2\}$ and $\{3, 4\}$ are disjoint because their intersection is empty.

flashcards.definition: The number of elements in set $A$.
The set that contains no elements.
A counting rule for the union of two sets: add the sizes and subtract the overlap.

questions.stem: Which symbol is used for the intersection of two sets?
questions.explanation: $A \cap B$ is read "$A$ intersection $B$" and contains only the elements shared by both sets.

questions.stem: Which symbol is used for the union of two sets?
questions.explanation: $A \cup B$ is read "$A$ union $B$" and contains every element that is in $A$, in $B$, or in both.
$A'$ is the complement of $A$, meaning all elements in the universal set $U$ that are not in $A$.
$A'$ contains every element of $U$ that is not in $A$, giving the odd numbers from $1$ to $9$.
The intersection contains only the elements that appear in both sets: $2$ and $3$.
The union contains every element that is in $A$ or $B$, listed without duplication: $1, 2, 3, 4$.

questions.stem: If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint sets, what is $A \cap B$?
questions.explanation: Disjoint sets have no common elements, so their intersection is the empty set.

choices: The circle for $A$ is completely inside the circle for $B$
The two circles do not touch
questions.explanation: When $A$ is a subset of $B$, every element of $A$ is also in $B$, so circle $A$ lies inside circle $B$.
Using $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$ gives $10 + 6 - 2 = 14$.

questions.stem: In a class of $40$ students, $25$ play tennis, $18$ play hockey and $8$ play both. How many play neither sport?
questions.explanation: Tennis only is $25 - 8 = 17$, hockey only is $18 - 8 = 10$, so $17 + 8 + 10 = 35$ play at least one sport. Therefore $40 - 35 = 5$ play neither.

questions.stem: Let $U = \{1, 2, 3, \dots, 20\}$. $A$ is the set of even numbers and $B$ is the set of multiples of $3$. How many elements are in $A \cap B$?
questions.explanation: $A \cap B$ contains multiples of $6$: $6, 12, 18$. That is $3$ elements.
The set contains natural numbers less than $6$, which are $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$.
A set and its complement have no elements in common, so their intersection is the empty set.

questions.stem: If $A \subset B$, which statement must be true?
questions.explanation: If every element of $A$ is in $B$, then $A$ and $B$ overlap exactly on $A$, and their union is just $B$.

questions.stem: In a survey of $50$ people, $30$ like tea, $25$ like coffee and $10$ like both. How many like at least one drink?
questions.explanation: Using inclusion-exclusion, $30 + 25 - 10 = 45$ people like tea, coffee, or both.
